answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From King’s sermon “Loving Your Enemies,” published in his 1963 collection Strength to Love. The lines sit inside the passage “Returning hate for hate multiplies hate, adding deeper darkness to a night already devoid of stars…” — confirmed genuine ↗.

source.heading: The passage in context
source.excerpt: Returning hate for hate multiplies hate, adding deeper darkness to a night already devoid of stars. Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.
trail: The line is genuine King, drawn from the sermon “Loving Your Enemies” in Strength to Love (1963) — Death Penalty Information Center ↗.
The two famous sentences, with a reflection on King’s light-and-darkness image, are also reproduced by the National Christian Foundation ↗.
A widely shared 2011 version begins with a sentence King never wrote; that opening line was authored by a Facebook user named Jessica Dovey — CBS News ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version drops the opening sentence about “deeper darkness”
source.excerptNote: King preached “Loving Your Enemies” in several settings in the late 1950s and early 1960s before publishing it in Strength to Love. The two famous sentences are almost always quoted alone, stripped of the “returning hate for hate” line that sets them up.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: About Martin Luther King Jr.
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was a Baptist minister and the foremost leader of the American civil rights movement, whose philosophy of nonviolent resistance was grounded in Christian agape love. Strength to Love (1963), a collection of his sermons, is where this line was published; its theme of answering hate with love runs through his entire public ministry. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

misattribution.heading: The real misquote here
misattribution.intro: The two sentences themselves are authentic King. The confusion is a different one: a version that went viral after Osama bin Laden’s death in May 2011 opened with a line King never wrote.

items.who: Martin Luther King Jr. (the “I will not rejoice” opening line)
items.why: The much-shared sentence “I mourn the loss of thousands of precious lives, but I will not rejoice in the death of one, not even an enemy” was written in 2011 by Jessica Dovey, a Penn State graduate teaching in Japan, as her own introduction to the real King quote. When her Facebook post was re-shared, the quotation marks dropped and her words were absorbed into King’s — CBS News ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: “Darkness cannot drive out darkness… hate cannot drive out hate” is real Martin Luther King Jr., from Strength to Love; only the “I will not rejoice” preamble that sometimes precedes it online is a later, mis-credited add-on — Christian Science Monitor ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: King built “Loving Your Enemies” around the idea that nonviolence is not passive but the only force capable of ending a cycle of retaliation. The darkness-and-light image makes the argument concrete: you cannot cancel a thing with more of the same — only its opposite will do.
Published in Strength to Love in 1963, at the height of the civil rights struggle, the sermon reframed loving one’s enemies not as sentimental weakness but as strategic and moral strength.
detailsBody: King preached versions of “Loving Your Enemies” on several occasions — including at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery and at Lenten services in Detroit — before it appeared in print. The Strength to Love text is the one most often cited today.
The passage draws on the Christian concept of agape — unconditional, redemptive goodwill — which King distinguished from mere affection or liking and made the moral engine of the nonviolent movement.
